title: At Three, This Indian-American Boy Became the World's Youngest Male Author
excerpt: Advay Jain of South Brunswick, New Jersey, wrote 'Dino Learns Not To Waste Food' at age three — earning a Guinness World Record and a felicitation from India's Consul General in New York.
body:
• Advay Jain, now 4, of South Brunswick, New Jersey, holds the Guinness World Record as the youngest male to publish a book — he was 3 years and 345 days old at publication.
  • His book, 'Dino Learns Not To Waste Food' (Panda Publishing Agency), grew out of his own preschool's no-outside-food rule; more than 1,300 copies have sold worldwide.
  • India's Consul General in New York, Binaya Srikanta Pradhan, felicitated Advay at his office, calling his work an inspiration for young readers everywhere.
  • Writing runs in the family: Advay's 12-year-old sister Avya is also a published author, of 'The Call of the Nether', as well as a painter.

At an age when most children are still learning to form sentences, Advay Jain wrote a book. The Indian-American preschooler from South Brunswick, New Jersey, has entered the Guinness World Records as the youngest male to publish a book — he was just 3 years and 345 days old when 'Dino Learns Not To Waste Food' was published earlier this year.

Now four, Advay was felicitated this week by India's Consul General in New York, Binaya Srikanta Pradhan, who welcomed him at the consulate office and congratulated him on the achievement. The recognition marks a remarkable chapter for a boy whose storytelling began with drawings on the walls of his home.

"Through his book 'Dino Learns Not to Waste Food,' Advay inspires young readers to value food and embrace the importance of avoiding food waste."

— Consulate General of India, New York

The story behind Dino

The idea for the book came from Advay's own life. When he moved to a new preschool, the school had a rule against bringing food from home — and the toddler noticed. According to reports from South Brunswick cited by The Times of India, that everyday adjustment sparked the story of Dino, a character who learns why wasting food matters. Published by Panda Publishing Agency, the book has sold more than 1,300 copies worldwide, a figure that is still growing, his father Neeraj Kumar said.

From walls to pages

Advay's storytelling began visually. He used to draw his ideas on the walls — and instead of stopping him, his parents helped channel the sketches into a fully developed book of drawings and short stories. He and his wife Sonal Bansal began turning Dino's story into a book in July 2025, a process that took ten months from first draft to print, Neeraj Kumar told local media.

A family of authors

The writing talent runs in the family. Advay's elder sister, 12-year-old Avya, is herself a published author — her book is titled 'The Call of the Nether' — and a painter. The siblings now share the unusual distinction of both being published writers before finishing elementary school.

A growing list of record-setting young authors

Advay joins a small but notable club of prodigies. Saarth Khanna Sohum of Singapore holds a Guinness World Record for the youngest published writer of a bilingual story, and Chryseis Knight — who wrote 'The Great Big Lion' at age three and was inducted into Mensa at two — counts among the youngest authors in the world. Each of these cases has drawn attention to how early creativity, when encouraged rather than corrected, can produce work that reaches readers.

What this means for the diaspora

For Indian-American families, Advay's story resonates on two levels: it is a point of community pride, and it is a parenting lesson. His parents' instinct — to build on the wall drawings rather than ban them — turned a toddler's imagination into a published book. It is a reminder that the raw material of creativity is already there in every child; it just needs a way onto the page.

What's next

The Consulate General said both Advay and Avya "continue to inspire young minds through their creativity and stories." With book sales climbing and a Guinness certificate on the shelf, the next chapter — a second book, perhaps, from a five-year-old — may not be far off.
